title: How to write a chase at each stage
content:
Every chase is short, names the invoice and the amount, and makes paying easier than replying. Reply on the original thread when one exists — a new email reads as a demand, a reply reads as a conversation.

**Reminder** (1-7 days past due). Assume it was missed, because it usually was. One line saying the invoice is now past due, the amount and the reference, the payment link, and an offer to resend the invoice. No deadline, no consequence, no chasing language at all.

**Follow-up** (8-21 days past due). Assume it is stuck somewhere and ask where. Name how far past due it is, ask whether it has reached their accounts payable, and ask for a date rather than a payment. A question that can be answered in five words gets answered.

**Firm** (22+ days past due). State the position without threatening. The invoice reference, the amount, the number of days outstanding, the agreed terms, and a request for a payment date this week. Say what happens next only if it is genuinely true and already agreed in the terms. Never invent a consequence, never mention debt collection unless a person has decided to, and never write in capitals.

Weigh the customer's history in every stage: an account that has always paid, just late, gets the gentler end of the stage; a first invoice that has never moved gets the firmer end. Read the installation settings included with this run and sign every draft with the configured 'sender_name'.

Draft only. The assistant never sends a chase itself.
